questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.1 Weight and balance effect on sUAS flight characteristics
questions.keyword: center of gravity forward aft effect stability control
questions.text: A remote pilot attaches a camera gimbal to the front of a small quadcopter, shifting the center of gravity (CG) significantly forward of the manufacturer's recommended range. During flight, the pilot notices the aircraft pitches nose-down and requires continuous aft stick input to maintain level flight. What is the primary risk of operating with a CG this far forward?

answers.text: The forward CG reduces motor RPM on the rear motors, causing asymmetric thrust that rotates the aircraft clockwise when viewed from above
A forward CG beyond limits can exhaust available nose-up control authority, making it impossible to arrest a pitch-down tendency, particularly at low speed or during maneuvers
The forward CG increases the effective payload weight reported to the flight controller, causing the altitude hold mode to climb uncontrollably
A forward CG improves penetration in headwind conditions and has no negative effect on multirotor aircraft, unlike fixed-wing aircraft

explanations.a: CG shift affects pitch balance and control authority, not differential motor RPM rotation direction; asymmetric thrust is a separate flight control concept.
explanations.b: When CG is forward of limits, the aircraft has a persistent nose-down tendency; if this nose-down moment exceeds the available nose-up (aft) control authority, the pilot loses the ability to maintain level flight or recover from a pitch-down attitude, which is particularly dangerous at low altitude.
explanations.c: The flight controller's altitude hold mode operates on barometric and/or GPS altitude data, not a weight report derived from CG position; this mechanism is fictitious.
explanations.d: CG limits apply to multirotor aircraft as well as fixed-wing; a CG outside limits can reduce or exhaust control authority in any aircraft type and is not beneficial.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.1 Weight and balance effect on sUAS flight characteristics
questions.keyword: aft CG instability uncommanded pitch up
questions.text: During preflight loading, a remote pilot installs a battery pack in the aft compartment of a fixed-wing sUAS, placing the CG behind the rear limit. The manufacturer's manual warns that aft CG operation is hazardous. What specific handling characteristic makes an aft CG condition particularly dangerous for this aircraft?

answers.text: An aft CG makes the aircraft longitudinally unstable, so pitch disturbances self-reinforce rather than self-correct, making recovery from pitch excursions difficult or impossible
An aft CG reduces the aircraft's maximum airspeed by increasing parasitic drag from the battery protruding into the airstream
An aft CG causes the aircraft to roll left because the weight imbalance torques the fuselage against the propeller thrust line
An aft CG locks the elevator in a nose-down position through a mechanical linkage moment that increases with airspeed

explanations.a: An aft CG reduces the restoring moment of the tail relative to the wing's pitching moment, making the aircraft longitudinally unstable; a pitch disturbance causes the nose to continue pitching in the disturbed direction rather than returning to level flight, and the situation can become unrecoverable.
explanations.b: CG position affects longitudinal stability, not parasitic drag from battery installation; drag concerns are separate from the primary handling hazard of aft CG.
explanations.c: An aft CG creates a pitch-up tendency due to the wing's lift acting forward of the CG, not a rolling tendency; roll is governed by lateral CG balance.
explanations.d: There is no mechanical elevator locking mechanism tied to CG position; the hazard is aerodynamic instability, not a physical control restriction.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.2 Effect of payload weight on sUAS performance
questions.keyword: overloading battery consumption flight time reduction
questions.text: A remote pilot normally operates a quadcopter with a 1-pound camera payload, achieving 22-minute flight times. For a new job, the pilot replaces the camera with a 2.5-pound thermal imaging unit. Assuming all other conditions are equal, how will this increased payload weight most likely affect sUAS performance?

answers.text: Flight time will increase because the additional weight reduces the sUAS's speed, causing the motors to operate in a more efficient low-RPM range
The sUAS will automatically limit altitude to compensate for the increased weight, with no effect on flight time or battery consumption
Flight time will decrease and battery consumption will increase because the motors must produce more thrust to support the greater total weight
Performance will be unchanged because the flight controller compensates for payload changes by redistributing motor torque among all four motors

explanations.a: Increased weight requires more thrust, which demands higher motor RPM and more current from the battery; flight time decreases, not increases, with heavier payloads.
explanations.b: Flight controllers do not automatically limit altitude based on weight; they attempt to maintain the commanded altitude regardless of payload, drawing more current as needed, which depletes the battery faster.
explanations.c: Greater payload weight increases the total weight the motors must lift; maintaining hover and controlled flight requires higher motor RPM and more current draw, directly reducing battery endurance and total flight time.
explanations.d: Flight controllers distribute torque among motors to manage attitude but cannot eliminate the fundamental physical requirement for more thrust to lift more weight; battery consumption will increase with the heavier payload.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.2 Effect of payload weight on sUAS performance
questions.keyword: max takeoff weight payload capacity calculation
questions.text: An sUAS has a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 15.4 pounds specified in the manufacturer's manual. The aircraft itself weighs 9.2 pounds with its standard battery installed. A client wants the pilot to carry a 6-pound sensor package. Can this payload be legally and safely accommodated?

answers.text: Yes, because 9.2 plus 6 equals 15.2 pounds, which is under the 15.4-pound MTOW, so the operation is within manufacturer limits
Yes, because the 55-pound Part 107 limit is the only weight constraint; manufacturer MTOW limits are advisory only and may be exceeded for commercial operations
No, because 9.2 plus 6 equals 15.2 pounds; while under MTOW, payloads over 5 pounds require a Part 107 payload waiver from the FAA
No, because 9.2 plus 6 equals 15.2 pounds, which exceeds the available payload margin of 15.4 minus 9.2 equals 6.2 pounds; however, 15.2 is under MTOW so the operation is within limits

explanations.a: Total weight of 9.2 + 6.0 = 15.2 lb is below the manufacturer's MTOW of 15.4 lb; the operation falls within the manufacturer's weight limits and the Part 107 55-lb ceiling; from a weight perspective this payload can be accommodated.
explanations.b: Manufacturer MTOW limits are not merely advisory; exceeding them violates the condition-for-safe-operation requirement of 14 CFR 107.15 and can lead to structural or performance failures.
explanations.c: Part 107 does not establish a 5-pound payload threshold requiring a waiver; payload weight is governed by the manufacturer's MTOW and the 55-lb Part 107 limit, not a separate payload waiver process.
explanations.d: The calculation 9.2 + 6.0 = 15.2 lb is correct and is indeed below the 15.4-lb MTOW; this answer is internally contradictory — it says 'No' but then confirms the operation is within limits; the correct conclusion is that the operation is permissible.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.3 Propeller selection and thrust effects
questions.keyword: propeller pitch diameter thrust efficiency altitude
questions.text: A remote pilot is reviewing two propeller options for an sUAS operating regularly at a field elevation of 6,000 ft MSL. Option A has a larger diameter and higher pitch; Option B has a smaller diameter and lower pitch. At high elevation where air density is reduced, which propeller characteristic generally produces more thrust per watt at altitude?

answers.text: Smaller diameter, lower pitch blades because they spin faster and compensate for thin air through increased RPM alone
Larger diameter, higher pitch blades because they move a larger volume of air per revolution, generating more thrust at lower RPM in thin air
Propeller geometry has no effect at altitude; thrust output depends exclusively on motor wattage and battery voltage, not blade dimensions
Smaller diameter blades are always preferred at altitude because they reduce gyroscopic precession effects that worsen with altitude

explanations.a: Simply increasing RPM does not offset reduced air density as efficiently as moving a larger volume of air per revolution; high-pitch, large-diameter blades are generally more efficient at altitude.
explanations.b: At higher altitudes with lower air density, larger diameter blades with higher pitch move more air mass per revolution and maintain thrust more effectively than smaller diameter blades; this is why high-altitude operations often use larger, lower-RPM propellers rather than smaller, faster-spinning ones.
explanations.c: Propeller geometry directly determines how efficiently the motor's mechanical energy is converted into thrust; blade design is a critical performance variable, especially at altitude where air density is reduced.
explanations.d: Gyroscopic precession effects relate to rotation speed and mass distribution, not altitude; this is not a standard propeller selection criterion for high-altitude sUAS operations.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.4 Battery performance and discharge rates
questions.keyword: LiPo battery temperature cold weather voltage sag capacity loss
questions.text: A remote pilot conducts an sUAS inspection flight in sub-freezing winter temperatures (−5°C / 23°F). After only 8 minutes of flight, the flight controller's low battery alarm activates, even though the battery showed 95% charge before launch. What is the most likely cause of this early battery depletion?

answers.text: Sub-freezing temperatures reduce lithium polymer (LiPo) battery capacity and increase internal resistance, causing rapid voltage sag and early low-voltage warnings
The flight controller's battery percentage display is miscalibrated in winter and consistently reads higher than actual charge in cold conditions
Cold air increases rotor efficiency so much that the motors draw twice the normal current to avoid over-speeding the aircraft in dense cold air
The sUAS navigation system uses more power in cold weather to maintain GPS lock, drawing down the battery faster than in warmer conditions

explanations.a: LiPo batteries experience significant capacity reduction and increased internal resistance at low temperatures; chemical reactions within the cells slow down, reducing available voltage and usable capacity; the battery may show a high resting charge but rapidly sags under load in cold conditions.
explanations.b: Battery percentage miscalibration is not the standard explanation for cold-weather early depletion; the primary cause is the well-documented electrochemical sensitivity of LiPo cells to low temperatures.
explanations.c: Cold, denser air does increase rotor efficiency somewhat, but this does not cause doubled current draw; the dominant cold-weather effect is battery capacity reduction, not increased motor current from over-speed protection.
explanations.d: GPS receivers do consume some power but not significantly more in cold weather; the GPS system is not the primary driver of cold-weather battery depletion in sUAS operations.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.4 Battery performance and discharge rates
questions.keyword: LiPo battery puffing swelling damage inspection pre-flight
questions.text: During a preflight inspection, a remote pilot notices that one of the LiPo battery packs appears visibly swollen, with the sides of the pack bulging outward noticeably. Under aeronautical decision-making principles and 14 CFR 107.15, what should the pilot do?

answers.text: Install the battery and conduct a brief 5-minute test flight to determine whether the swelling affects actual flight performance before making a go/no-go decision
Ground the sUAS and remove the swollen battery from service; a puffed LiPo poses a fire and explosion hazard and should be disposed of according to applicable regulations
Apply duct tape over the swollen area to reinforce the battery casing and prevent further expansion during the flight
Proceed with the flight if the swelling is less than 5 millimeters because minor puffing is considered within normal LiPo tolerance by most manufacturers

explanations.a: A visibly swollen LiPo must be removed from service immediately; flying with a puffed LiPo risks in-flight fire, explosion, or catastrophic failure, none of which can be safely assessed with a test flight.
explanations.b: LiPo battery puffing (swelling) indicates internal gas production from cell degradation, overcharging, or damage; a puffed LiPo is at elevated risk of thermal runaway and fire; the battery must be removed from service and disposed of per applicable hazardous materials regulations.
explanations.c: Taping a swollen LiPo does not address the underlying chemical instability and could trap heat, increasing the risk of thermal runaway; this is not an acceptable mitigation.
explanations.d: There is no industry-standard 5 mm swelling tolerance for LiPo packs; any visible puffing is a disqualifying defect requiring the battery to be removed from service.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.5 Performance charts and hover ceiling
questions.keyword: hover ceiling in-ground effect out-of-ground effect HIGE HOGE
questions.text: A remote pilot is assessing whether an sUAS can maintain a stable hover at 400 ft AGL at an operating site with a density altitude of 5,800 ft. The manufacturer's performance chart shows a hover ceiling out-of-ground effect (HOGE) of 6,200 ft density altitude at MTOW. What does this data indicate about the planned operation?

answers.text: The 400 ft AGL hover is not possible because the density altitude of 5,800 ft exceeds the allowable 400 ft AGL ceiling by a factor greater than ten
The HOGE ceiling is irrelevant at 400 ft AGL because all hover ceiling data applies exclusively to operations above 1,000 ft AGL
The hover ceiling data applies only to the first 10 minutes of flight; after 10 minutes the HOGE ceiling drops by 50% due to battery depletion
The sUAS can maintain the 400 ft AGL hover because the density altitude of 5,800 ft is below the HOGE ceiling of 6,200 ft, confirming adequate performance margin

explanations.a: The 400 ft AGL is the height above ground, not a performance ceiling; the comparison is between density altitude (5,800 ft) and the HOGE ceiling (6,200 ft); since 5,800 ft is below 6,200 ft, a hover is achievable.
explanations.b: HOGE ceiling applies to all out-of-ground-effect hover altitudes; it is not restricted to operations above 1,000 ft AGL.
explanations.c: Performance charts typically reflect sustained hover capability, not a time-limited 10-minute window; battery depletion is a separate consideration from the density altitude hover ceiling.
explanations.d: The HOGE ceiling represents the maximum density altitude at which the sUAS can sustain a hover without ground effect cushion; at the planned density altitude of 5,800 ft, which is 400 ft below the HOGE ceiling of 6,200 ft, the sUAS has adequate performance margin to maintain the planned hover.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.5 Performance charts and hover ceiling
questions.keyword: ground effect sUAS rotor close to surface efficiency benefit
questions.text: A remote pilot is launching an sUAS from ground level and notices that during the initial low hover at 1–2 feet AGL, the aircraft feels more stable and requires less throttle to maintain altitude than at 10 feet AGL. What aerodynamic phenomenon explains this difference in performance close to the ground?

answers.text: The Venturi effect accelerates airflow under the aircraft between the rotors and the ground, creating additional lift at low altitude
The aircraft's GPS altitude hold system automatically reduces motor output near the ground to prevent ground strikes, artificially reducing power draw
Solar radiation reflected from the ground surface heats the air under the rotor disk, lowering its density and increasing lift efficiency within 2 feet of the surface
Ground effect reduces the induced velocity through the rotor disk by interrupting the recirculation of downwash, requiring less power to generate the same thrust close to the ground

explanations.a: While airflow between rotors and the ground is affected by proximity, the Venturi effect is not the primary mechanism of ground effect for rotor systems.
explanations.b: GPS altitude hold systems do not artificially reduce motor output near the ground as an anti-collision measure; the perceived performance difference near the ground is real aerodynamic ground effect.
explanations.c: Solar radiation reflection is not a recognized mechanism of rotor ground effect; ground effect is an aerodynamic interference phenomenon, not a thermal one.
explanations.d: Ground effect occurs when a rotor operates close enough to the surface that the ground interrupts the downward flow of recirculated air, reducing induced velocity through the rotor disk; this makes the rotor more efficient — it generates more lift per unit of power — explaining the reduced throttle requirement and increased stability close to the ground.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.6 Vortex ring state conditions and avoidance
questions.keyword: vortex ring state settling with power symptoms recognition
questions.text: During a steep descent at low airspeed, an sUAS remote pilot notices that the aircraft begins descending faster than commanded despite the throttle being increased to arrest the rate of descent. The descent rate continues to increase with more power. What condition has the aircraft entered, and what is the correct recovery action?

answers.text: The aircraft has entered a motor overspeed condition; the recovery is to cut throttle immediately and allow the aircraft to autorotate to the surface
The aircraft has activated its geofencing descent mode triggered by a GPS altitude error; the recovery is to cycle the flight mode selector to manual override
The aircraft has encountered a sudden microburst downdraft; the recovery is to climb immediately at full throttle in the vertical axis until the downdraft boundary is crossed

The aircraft has entered vortex ring state (settling with power), where the rotors are operating in their own recirculated downwash; recovery requires moving forward or laterally to allow the rotors to encounter undisturbed air

explanations.a: Vortex ring state is not an overspeed condition; cutting throttle would accelerate the descent and worsen the outcome; the aircraft requires lateral or forward movement to exit the recirculated airflow.
explanations.b: Geofencing descent modes are manufacturer-specific software functions and not the explanation for the described aerodynamic symptom pattern; the description of worsening descent with increasing power is characteristic of vortex ring state.
explanations.c: A microburst downdraft is an external weather phenomenon; VRS is an aerodynamic condition self-induced by the rotor; in VRS, climbing vertically at full throttle worsens the condition rather than providing recovery.
explanations.d: Vortex ring state (VRS), also called settling with power, occurs when an aircraft descends vertically at low airspeed into its own rotor downwash, causing the rotor to operate in recirculated air with reduced efficiency; adding power worsens the condition; recovery requires moving the aircraft out of the recirculated air column by transitioning to forward or lateral flight.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.6 Vortex ring state conditions and avoidance
questions.keyword: vortex ring state avoidance descent rate approach angle caution
questions.text: To avoid vortex ring state (VRS) during descent operations, which combination of flight parameters should a remote pilot monitor and maintain?

answers.text: Keep descent rates high and airspeeds low to maximize rotor disk loading and prevent the onset of recirculated downwash
Keep the sUAS at altitudes above 400 ft AGL during all descent maneuvers, which prevents VRS by maintaining rotor efficiency in undisturbed air
Always descend with throttle at 100% to keep the rotors spinning fast enough to prevent recirculation of downwash through the disk
Maintain a forward airspeed component during descent rather than descending vertically at low speed, keeping descent rate within manufacturer limits

explanations.a: High descent rates and low airspeeds are precisely the conditions that promote VRS onset; this is the opposite of a safe approach.
explanations.b: VRS risk is related to flight technique, not to a specific altitude band; the condition can occur at any altitude where the described low-airspeed, high-descent-rate conditions exist.
explanations.c: Full throttle in a vertical descent contributes to VRS; reducing airspeed while maintaining high power is a contributing factor, not a preventive one.
explanations.d: VRS requires specific conditions: low or zero airspeed combined with a high descent rate; maintaining forward airspeed during descent prevents the aircraft from settling into its own downwash; following manufacturer descent rate limits and avoiding steep, slow, vertical descents are the primary VRS avoidance strategies.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.7 Effect of wind on range and endurance
questions.keyword: headwind groundspeed range endurance trade-off
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning a one-way corridor inspection flight of 2 miles into a 15-knot headwind. The sUAS has a cruise airspeed of 25 knots and a maximum flight time of 18 minutes at that airspeed. How does the headwind affect the range and required battery capacity for this mission?

answers.text: The headwind has no effect on range because the sUAS flies at a constant airspeed; only groundspeed changes and the motors do not use additional power
The headwind eliminates the ability to return to the launch point because the sUAS cannot maintain altitude while fighting the wind
The headwind reduces motor efficiency and doubles battery consumption regardless of mission distance or flight duration

The headwind reduces groundspeed from 25 to 10 knots, extending the time needed to cover the 2-mile distance to approximately 12 minutes, using more of the available battery capacity for the outbound leg

explanations.a: Headwinds reduce groundspeed, which increases the time to cover a fixed distance; although airspeed stays the same, the longer time aloft consumes more battery capacity for the same ground distance.
explanations.b: A 25-knot airspeed is sufficient to make headway against a 15-knot wind; the sUAS has 10 knots of positive groundspeed and can complete the return trip.
explanations.c: Headwinds do not double battery consumption independent of distance; the relationship is between groundspeed, distance, and time, not a fixed multiplier.
explanations.d: With a 15-knot headwind and 25-knot airspeed, groundspeed is 25 − 15 = 10 knots; at 10 knots groundspeed, covering 2 miles takes approximately 12 minutes, compared to about 4.8 minutes with no wind; this significantly increases the battery used on the outbound leg and must be factored into flight planning.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.7 Effect of wind on range and endurance
questions.keyword: tailwind return leg battery reserves mission planning
questions.text: A remote pilot plans a round-trip sUAS survey mission of 1 mile out and 1 mile back. The wind is 20 knots directly on the nose for the outbound leg. The pilot wisely plans to fly outbound first into the headwind. Why is this preferable to flying with the tailwind first?

answers.text: Flying into the headwind first allows the motors to warm up gradually against resistance before the more demanding tailwind return leg
Flying into the headwind first is only preferable when operating in Class G airspace; tailwind-first departures are required in controlled airspace by ATC procedures
Flying into the headwind first reduces the risk of exceeding the 87-knot groundspeed limit because the wind counters the aircraft's airspeed on the outbound leg

Flying into the headwind first while battery charge is highest ensures the aircraft can fight the wind on the outbound leg; the tailwind return requires less energy and uses the remaining battery more efficiently

explanations.a: Motor warm-up is not a standard sUAS flight planning concept; electric motors do not require a gradual warm-up period analogous to internal combustion engines.
explanations.b: Wind direction planning is not differentiated by airspace class; the energy conservation principle applies regardless of airspace class.
explanations.c: 87-knot groundspeed concerns apply to sUAS that might approach that limit; a 20-knot tailwind added to typical sUAS airspeeds would not approach 87 knots for most aircraft, making this a marginal consideration not the primary planning reason.
explanations.d: Flying into the headwind while the battery is freshest ensures enough power reserves to overcome wind resistance on the more energy-demanding outbound leg; the tailwind return requires less thrust to cover the same ground distance in less time, using battery reserves efficiently and ensuring enough charge to reach home base.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.1 Weight and balance effect on sUAS flight characteristics
questions.keyword: lateral CG asymmetric loading roll tendency correction
questions.text: A remote pilot installs a sensor package that is mounted 6 inches to the right of the sUAS centerline, creating a lateral CG offset. During hover, the aircraft rolls right and requires continuous left correction from the remote pilot. Under aeronautical principles, what is the best corrective action before the next flight?

answers.text: Increase the right-side motor output percentages in the flight controller calibration menu to compensate for the added left-roll correction needed
The condition is normal and requires no correction because all multirotor flight controllers apply automatic lateral trim during the first hover of each session
Fly with a higher-than-normal altitude to allow the autopilot more control authority to manage the asymmetric loading
Reposition the payload to reduce the lateral CG offset, or add ballast to the left side to rebalance the aircraft within the manufacturer's lateral CG limits

explanations.a: Adjusting individual motor output through calibration menus is a software workaround that does not address the physical CG imbalance; it may also create unpredictable control responses and reduce available control authority in other axes.
explanations.b: Most flight controllers apply basic trim settings during calibration, but they do not automatically detect and fully correct for persistent lateral CG offsets caused by asymmetric payloads; continuous roll correction signals a genuine loading problem.
explanations.c: Higher altitude does not increase lateral control authority in a meaningful way; the physical CG imbalance requires a physical correction.
explanations.d: The correct solution to a lateral CG imbalance is to physically reposition the payload closer to the CG centerline or add counterbalancing ballast; this addresses the root cause rather than masking the problem with software adjustments.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.8 Performance degradation factors — humidity and temperature
questions.keyword: high humidity reduced air density lift effect sUAS
questions.text: A remote pilot operates on a hot, humid summer day. A colleague suggests that high humidity should be ignored because 'water is heavier than air.' How should the remote pilot correctly understand the effect of high humidity on sUAS performance?

answers.text: The colleague is correct; humid air contains water vapor which increases air density, generating more lift and improving sUAS performance on hot days
Humidity has no measurable effect on sUAS performance because propeller thrust is driven by RPM, which is independent of air composition
High humidity reduces air density because water vapor (H₂O, molecular weight 18) displaces heavier nitrogen and oxygen molecules, resulting in less dense air and degraded sUAS performance
High humidity increases rotor efficiency by lubricating the blade surface, reducing boundary layer separation and increasing the lift coefficient of each blade

explanations.a: The misconception that humid air is denser than dry air is common but incorrect; while liquid water is denser, water vapor in the atmosphere is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules it displaces.
explanations.b: Propeller thrust is directly proportional to air density; an RPM-based independence from air composition is incorrect — the same RPM produces less thrust in less dense air.
explanations.c: Water vapor has a molecular weight of 18 g/mol, while nitrogen (28 g/mol) and oxygen (32 g/mol) are significantly heavier; when water vapor displaces these molecules in the air, the resulting mixture is less dense; less dense air reduces rotor efficiency and sUAS performance, which is why high temperature and humidity together elevate density altitude.
explanations.d: Rotor blade efficiency is aerodynamically governed by air density and blade geometry; humidity does not lubricate blade surfaces or increase lift coefficient.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.3 Propeller selection and thrust effects
questions.keyword: damaged propeller vibration structural fatigue failure risk
questions.text: During a preflight inspection, a remote pilot notices a small nick approximately 3 mm deep along the leading edge of one propeller blade. The other blades appear undamaged. Under 14 CFR 107.15 and performance principles, should the pilot fly with this propeller?

answers.text: Yes, because a 3 mm nick is within the allowable tolerance for small recreational sUAS propellers under advisory circular guidance
Yes, if the flight is limited to hover-only operations below 50 ft AGL where propeller loads are minimal
No, a nick changes the blade's aerodynamic profile and creates an imbalance that generates vibration, which can cause structural fatigue, premature bearing failure, and reduced control authority
Yes, provided the nicked blade is rotated to the most aerodynamically favorable position relative to the other blades before flight

explanations.a: There is no FAA advisory circular establishing a 3 mm nick tolerance for sUAS propellers; 14 CFR 107.15 requires the sUAS to be in a condition for safe operation, and a nicked propeller does not meet this standard.
explanations.b: Restricting to hover does not eliminate propeller imbalance issues; vibration from an imbalanced blade occurs throughout all flight regimes and accelerates bearing and frame wear even at low altitude.
explanations.c: A nick on a propeller blade alters its aerodynamic shape, reducing lift on the damaged blade and creating aerodynamic imbalance; this imbalance generates vibration that stresses motor bearings, the airframe, and payload mounts; the propeller must be replaced before flight to ensure airworthiness.
explanations.d: Rotating the damaged blade to a different position does not restore its aerodynamic profile or eliminate imbalance; replacing the propeller is the required action.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.4 Battery performance and discharge rates
questions.keyword: LiPo storage voltage 3.85V per cell long term storage
questions.text: A remote pilot will not fly for three weeks and wants to properly store their LiPo batteries. The batteries are currently at full charge (4.2 V per cell). What is the recommended storage practice for LiPo batteries to maintain their long-term health?

answers.text: Store the batteries fully charged (4.2 V/cell) to ensure maximum capacity is available when flying resumes after the storage period
Discharge the batteries completely to 0 V before storage to prevent the self-discharge phenomenon that damages cells during prolonged storage
Discharge or charge the batteries to approximately 3.8–3.85 V per cell (storage charge) and store them in a cool, dry location away from flammable materials
Freeze the batteries at −20°C to halt electrochemical reactions and preserve maximum capacity throughout the storage period

explanations.a: Storing LiPo batteries at full charge (4.2 V/cell) for extended periods accelerates electrolyte degradation and reduces long-term capacity; full charge is appropriate immediately before use, not for storage.
explanations.b: Fully discharging a LiPo below the minimum voltage threshold causes irreversible cell damage and can render the battery unsafe or unusable; complete discharge is never the recommended storage procedure.
explanations.c: The recommended LiPo storage voltage of approximately 3.8–3.85 V per cell represents a partial charge state that minimizes electrochemical stress; storing at this voltage in a cool, dry environment significantly extends battery lifespan and maintains cell health during the storage period.
explanations.d: Freezing LiPo batteries can damage the electrolyte and separator materials; the recommended storage environment is cool (15–25°C) and dry, not frozen.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.9 Load factor and flight maneuver effects
questions.keyword: banked turn increased load factor effective weight structural stress
questions.text: A remote pilot executes a 60-degree banked turn with an sUAS during a commercial inspection. The manufacturer's maximum load factor is listed as 1.5G. What is the load factor experienced in a 60-degree banked level turn, and does it exceed the manufacturer's limit?

answers.text: The load factor in a 60-degree bank is 1.41G (√2), which is below the 1.5G limit and within the manufacturer's structural envelope
The load factor in a 60-degree bank is 1.0G because the rotors compensate for the bank angle and the effective weight remains equal to actual weight
The load factor in a 60-degree bank is 2G (1/cos 60°), which exceeds the 1.5G manufacturer limit and stresses the structure beyond its design envelope
Load factor in a banked turn applies only to fixed-wing aircraft; multirotor sUAS experience no load factor change in banked turns due to their thrust vector control

explanations.a: The load factor in a 60-degree bank is 1/cos 60° = 1/0.5 = 2.0G, not √2; √2 ≈ 1.41G corresponds to a 45-degree bank angle.
explanations.b: Load factor in a banked turn is a real physical phenomenon affecting multirotor aircraft; the rotors must produce more thrust to maintain altitude in a bank because only the vertical component of their thrust vector supports the weight, not the full thrust.
explanations.c: In a level banked turn, load factor = 1/cos(bank angle); at 60 degrees, this equals 1/cos 60° = 1/0.5 = 2.0G; this exceeds the manufacturer's 1.5G structural limit and risks structural damage to the airframe, motors, or propellers.
explanations.d: Load factor from banked flight affects multirotor sUAS just as it does fixed-wing aircraft; the physics of circular flight require increased thrust and impose higher loads on the structure regardless of aircraft type.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.1 Weight and balance effect on sUAS flight characteristics
questions.keyword: weight balance check arms moment calculation CG computation
questions.text: A fixed-wing sUAS has a reference datum at the nose. The wing generates lift at a point 18 inches aft of the datum, and the battery (1.8 lb) is installed at 8 inches aft of the datum. The airframe without battery weighs 4.5 lb with its CG at 20 inches aft. What is the loaded CG in inches aft of the datum?

answers.text: Approximately 16.6 inches aft of the datum, calculated by dividing total moment by total weight
Approximately 22.4 inches aft of the datum, calculated by summing all moments and dividing by total weight
14 inches aft of the datum, calculated by averaging the battery position (8 inches) and the airframe CG (20 inches)
18 inches aft of the datum, which equals the lift point and indicates perfect CG-to-lift alignment regardless of weight

explanations.a: CG = total moment / total weight. Airframe moment: 4.5 lb × 20 in = 90 in-lb. Battery moment: 1.8 lb × 8 in = 14.4 in-lb. Total moment: 104.4 in-lb. Total weight: 4.5 + 1.8 = 6.3 lb. CG = 104.4 / 6.3 ≈ 16.6 inches aft of the datum.
explanations.b: 22.4 inches is too far aft; the correct calculation (104.4 in-lb / 6.3 lb) yields approximately 16.6 inches.
explanations.c: Simple averaging of two CG positions without weighting by their respective weights is not the correct CG calculation method; moments must account for each component's weight.
explanations.d: The lift point does not automatically become the CG; these are independent values, and CG must be calculated from component weights and moment arms.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.8 Performance degradation factors — humidity and temperature
questions.keyword: hot day performance planning reduced hover time payload limit
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning an afternoon survey flight on a day when the temperature at the 4,000-ft MSL field is 37°C (99°F). Compared to a standard day (15°C at sea level), which performance adjustments should the pilot make?

answers.text: No adjustments are necessary because sUAS flight controllers automatically compensate for temperature and altitude through closed-loop motor feedback
Increase maximum payload weight by 10% to take advantage of the increased motor efficiency in warm, dry air at altitude
Plan for reduced hover endurance, lower payload capacity, and possible reduced maximum airspeed; consider flying earlier in the day when temperatures are cooler
Increase minimum battery reserves from 20% to 25% SOC only; no other adjustments are required for standard summer afternoon operations

explanations.a: Flight controllers do maintain rotor speed through feedback control but cannot create thrust that the air density does not support; automatic compensation does not eliminate performance penalties from high density altitude.
explanations.b: Warm, low-density air degrades rather than improves motor efficiency; increasing payload in these conditions would further stress the system.
explanations.c: High temperature at altitude significantly elevates density altitude; this reduces air density, decreases rotor efficiency and thrust margin, shortens hover endurance (higher motor current draw), and reduces available payload capacity; planning for these limitations and flying during cooler morning hours are appropriate risk management steps.
explanations.d: While conservative battery reserves are always wise, limiting adjustments to a 5% increase in reserve SOC fails to account for the significant performance degradation from high density altitude on a hot afternoon.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.2 Effect of payload weight on sUAS performance
questions.keyword: payload release in-flight weight change altitude unexpected climb
questions.text: An sUAS equipped with a payload release mechanism drops a 1.2-pound package during a delivery operation while maintaining a throttle setting calibrated for the original total weight. What will most likely happen to the aircraft immediately after the package is released?

answers.text: The sUAS will immediately descend because the loss of downward payload weight removes the stabilizing downward force and the rotors can no longer maintain lift equilibrium
Nothing changes immediately because the flight controller detects the weight change and reduces throttle to maintain altitude within 0.1 seconds
The sUAS will climb suddenly because the thrust that was supporting the payload's weight now exceeds the reduced total weight, creating a net upward force
The sUAS will roll left because the release mechanism is typically installed on the left side, creating a sudden lateral weight shift

explanations.a: Removing a downward payload weight reduces total weight; with unchanged thrust (throttle held constant), the net upward force increases and the aircraft climbs, not descends.
explanations.b: While modern flight controllers with fast altitude hold loops can respond quickly, the initial physical response is a momentary climb before the controller can compensate; the question asks what will 'most likely happen immediately.'
explanations.c: When a payload is released, total weight decreases instantly; if the throttle remains set for the pre-release weight, the motors are producing more thrust than needed to hover the lighter aircraft, resulting in a sudden climb; the remote pilot should anticipate this and reduce throttle at the moment of release.
explanations.d: The release mechanism location relative to CG may cause minor attitude changes, but the dominant effect of releasing significant weight with constant throttle is a vertical climb, not a roll.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.9 Load factor and flight maneuver effects
questions.keyword: rapid deceleration pitch-up increased load structural consideration
questions.text: A remote pilot rapidly pitches the sUAS nose up from horizontal cruise at 25 knots to arrest forward motion quickly. During this abrupt maneuver, what structural consideration is most significant?

answers.text: The rapid pitch-up reduces load factor momentarily because the rotors' thrust vector is redirected away from vertical during the pitching maneuver
The rapid pitch-up can impose elevated load factors on the airframe, motor mounts, and propellers beyond what steady-state flight produces, potentially exceeding structural limits
Rapid pitch-up maneuvers are always within structural limits for sUAS because the FAA requires all sUAS to withstand a minimum 3G load factor in any flight attitude
The structural loading during a rapid pitch-up is determined only by the payload weight; the airframe components experience no additional stress from abrupt control inputs

explanations.a: Rapid pitch-up maneuvers typically increase load factor momentarily rather than reducing it; redirecting thrust does not reduce structural loading during an abrupt deceleration.
explanations.b: Abrupt control inputs, particularly rapid pitch changes at airspeed, impose dynamic loads (load factors greater than 1G) on the airframe, motor mounts, and propellers; these instantaneous loads can exceed the structural design envelope if the maneuver is aggressive enough, and pilots should apply smooth, gradual inputs to stay within structural limits.
explanations.c: The FAA does not establish a universal 3G structural requirement for all sUAS; structural limits vary by aircraft design and are specified by the manufacturer; some lightweight sUAS have relatively low structural limits.
explanations.d: Airframe structural loading is affected by dynamic flight maneuvers, not only by payload weight; abrupt inputs create additional inertial loads on all structural components regardless of payload.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.4 Battery performance and discharge rates
questions.keyword: battery C-rating continuous discharge rate current capacity
questions.text: A remote pilot's LiPo battery is rated at 5,000 mAh with a 25C continuous discharge rate. During a demanding flight with the sUAS drawing peak currents, the pilot wants to know the maximum continuous current draw the battery is rated to supply. What is the battery's rated continuous discharge current?

answers.text: 125 amps, calculated by multiplying 5,000 mAh by 25C (5 Ah × 25 = 125 A)
200 amps, calculated by multiplying the voltage (typically 22.2 V for a 6S pack) by the C-rating
5,025 mAh, calculated by adding the capacity and C-rating together as if they were additive units
25 amps, calculated by dividing the C-rating by the capacity in amp-hours

explanations.a: Battery C-rating represents the multiple of the battery's capacity that can be discharged continuously; for a 5,000 mAh (5 Ah) battery at 25C: 5 Ah × 25 = 125 A maximum continuous discharge current; this is the fundamental C-rating calculation.
explanations.b: Voltage is not part of the C-rating calculation for discharge current; C-rating × capacity in amp-hours gives current in amperes, independent of voltage.
explanations.c: mAh and C-rating cannot be added as they are different units representing different physical quantities; this calculation is dimensionally incorrect.
explanations.d: Dividing the C-rating by capacity would give an incorrect and dimensionally inconsistent result; the correct formula is capacity (in Ah) multiplied by the C-rating to obtain current in amperes.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.7 Effect of wind on range and endurance
questions.keyword: effective endurance battery reserve 20 percent rule conservative planning
questions.text: A remote pilot's sUAS has a manufacturer-stated maximum flight time of 25 minutes in ideal calm conditions. Best practices for flight planning recommend maintaining a battery reserve. If the pilot conservatively plans to land with 20% battery capacity remaining, what is the effective usable flight time available for mission planning?

answers.text: 20 minutes, because 20% of 25 minutes (5 minutes) is subtracted from the total as the battery reserve
5 minutes, because only 20% of the total flight time is considered safe for mission planning under the reserve rule
25 minutes, because manufacturer flight times already include all required battery reserves at the time of certification
22 minutes, because 20% reserves apply only to flights over water or at night and standard land flights retain the full flight time

explanations.a: If the maximum flight time is 25 minutes and a 20% reserve is maintained, the reserve time is 0.20 × 25 = 5 minutes; usable mission time = 25 − 5 = 20 minutes for planning purposes.
explanations.b: Only 20% of total flight time (5 minutes) being usable would mean 80% is reserve, which dramatically over-reserves; the correct calculation leaves 80% (20 minutes) for the mission.
explanations.c: Manufacturer-stated flight times represent performance under specific test conditions and do not incorporate a safety reserve for operational use; the pilot must apply the reserve independently.
explanations.d: Battery reserves are a general best practice applicable to all operations regardless of terrain or time of day; the 20% reserve is not limited to water or night operations.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.5 Performance charts and hover ceiling
questions.keyword: manufacturer performance data accuracy real-world degradation
questions.text: A remote pilot reviews the manufacturer's published performance data for their sUAS, which lists a 30-minute hover endurance at MTOW under standard conditions. During actual operations, the pilot consistently achieves only 22–23 minutes. Which factors most likely explain this real-world performance gap?

answers.text: The manufacturer's data is always fraudulently inflated; all sUAS manufacturers are required by FAA regulation to publish optimistic performance figures

Manufacturer data is typically measured under ideal laboratory conditions; real-world degradation factors include battery age, wind, non-standard temperature and altitude, payload variations, and aggressive maneuvers
The FAA requires manufacturers to publish performance data that includes a 30% safety margin, meaning actual performance should be 30% better than published figures
The performance gap is caused exclusively by blade erosion from normal propeller wear; replacing the propellers every flight restores manufacturer-specified performance

explanations.a: Performance data discrepancies are not the result of regulatory-required inflation or manufacturer fraud; they reflect the difference between controlled test conditions and real-world operational variability.
explanations.b: Manufacturer-published performance data is typically collected under ideal conditions: calm winds, standard sea-level temperature and pressure, new batteries at peak capacity; in real operations, battery aging, wind resistance, temperature extremes, altitude, payload weight variations, and flight maneuvers all reduce endurance below the theoretical maximum.
explanations.c: The FAA does not require a 30% safety margin to be embedded in published performance figures; the gap between published and actual performance reflects real environmental and operational factors.
explanations.d: While propeller condition affects performance, multiple factors contribute to the performance gap; blade erosion alone is not the complete explanation, and replacing propellers every flight is not a standard practice.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.8 Performance degradation factors — humidity and temperature
questions.keyword: performance chart interpolation between data points altitude temperature
questions.text: A remote pilot's sUAS performance chart shows hover endurance of 20 minutes at a density altitude of 2,000 ft and 15 minutes at a density altitude of 4,000 ft. The planned operation will take place at a density altitude of 3,000 ft. Using linear interpolation, what is the estimated hover endurance at 3,000 ft density altitude?

answers.text: Approximately 17.5 minutes, interpolated midway between 20 and 15 minutes at the midpoint density altitude of 3,000 ft
20 minutes, because performance charts always round up to the nearest listed data point
15 minutes, because a conservative pilot always uses the lower adjacent data point for all mission planning
22 minutes, because performance improves linearly with altitude and 3,000 ft is below the peak efficiency point

explanations.a: Linear interpolation between 2,000 ft (20 min) and 4,000 ft (15 min): the midpoint 3,000 ft is exactly halfway; interpolated value = 20 + (15 − 20) × (3,000 − 2,000) / (4,000 − 2,000) = 20 − 2.5 = 17.5 minutes.
explanations.b: Performance charts do not round up to adjacent data points; interpolation is the standard method for determining values between published data points.
explanations.c: While conservatism in planning is wise, using the lower data point directly without interpolation would underestimate available endurance at 3,000 ft; interpolation provides a more accurate estimate while additional safety reserves can be applied separately.
explanations.d: Performance degrades with increasing density altitude (less dense air = less thrust per RPM); endurance decreases with altitude, not increases; 22 minutes is above the lower-density-altitude value and is directionally incorrect.

questions.name: Loading and Performance
questions.objective: 6.6 Vortex ring state conditions and avoidance
questions.keyword: vortex ring state slow vertical descent recirculated downwash
questions.text: Which combination of flight conditions is most likely to induce vortex ring state (VRS) in a multirotor sUAS?

answers.text: High forward airspeed descent at full throttle over flat terrain in calm wind conditions
Slow vertical descent at low airspeed with power applied, such as descending directly above the landing point while maintaining hover
Rapid horizontal acceleration at maximum airspeed in turbulent air near a line of trees
Hovering in strong crosswinds above a reflective water surface on a hot, humid day

explanations.a: High forward airspeed prevents the rotor from descending into its own recirculated downwash; VRS requires low or zero airspeed to develop.
explanations.b: VRS is induced when the aircraft descends vertically at low airspeed while the rotors are powered; the downwash from the rotors recirculates back up through the disk, reducing efficiency and causing an uncontrolled descent; slow vertical descent directly above the landing point is a classic VRS trigger scenario.
explanations.c: Rapid horizontal acceleration and high airspeeds prevent recirculation of rotor downwash; VRS does not develop in forward flight at significant airspeed.
explanations.d: Crosswinds, water surface reflections, and humid air are not factors that individually induce VRS; VRS is specifically an aerodynamic phenomenon requiring low-airspeed vertical descent with power applied.
